blocks.text: An AI agent cannot browse the web on its own. It needs a tool that goes out, runs a search, and brings back something useful.
A web search MCP server wraps a real search API behind two simple tools, one that searches and one that fetches a full page.
This lesson builds that server piece by piece, including the parts people forget, rate limits, cost per query, and proper citations.
1. Why Wrap Web Search in MCP

blocks.alt: Why Wrap Web Search in MCP
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590219-842426332.png
Search engines already expose APIs, so the value of an MCP wrapper is not the search itself, it is the contract.
MCP gives the model a stable, documented tool interface instead of a raw HTTP API it has to guess how to call.
It also gives you, the server owner, one place to enforce limits, log usage, and control cost before a request ever reaches the search provider.
That single choke point is what makes the rest of this lesson possible, every safeguard below hangs off that one entry point.
2. What the Search Tool Should Return
A search tool should return a short, ranked list of results, not a wall of raw HTML or a single best guess answer.
Each result needs three things at minimum, a title, a url, and a snippet that gives the model enough context to judge relevance.
Keeping the snippet short matters, the model reads many of these at once and a bloated snippet burns context for no real gain.
3. Designing the search Tool Schema
The schema should ask for a query string and, optionally, a result count and a recency filter.
Capping max_results at the schema level stops the model from asking for a hundred results and blowing the cost budget in one call.

blocks.title: Enums beat free text
blocks.content: The recency field is an enum, not a free string, so the model cannot send an unparseable value the provider would reject.

blocks.text: 4. Calling the Search API for Real Results
Inside the tool handler, the server calls the underlying provider, normalizes its response, and ranks the results before returning them.
Notice the server, not the model, decides the final result count, that keeps behavior predictable even if the provider ignores the limit.
5. Ranking and Filtering Results
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590221-839994773.png
Raw provider order is not always the best order for an agent, some providers mix in ads or low quality pages.

items: Drop results whose domain is on a known low quality or spam list.
De-duplicate near identical urls that only differ by tracking parameters.
Boost results with a clear publish date when recency was requested.
Cap the snippet length so no single result dominates the response.

blocks.text: A little filtering here saves the model from wasting a follow up fetch_page call on a page that was never worth reading.
6. The fetch_page Tool for Full Content

blocks.alt: The fetch_page Tool for Full Content
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590221-226589826.png
A snippet is often not enough, so the server also offers a second tool, fetch_page, that pulls the full readable content from one url.
This tool should only accept urls that came from a prior search result, or at least log clearly when it did not.

blocks.title: Keep fetch_page separate from search
blocks.content: Bundling fetching into search would force every query to pay the cost of downloading full pages even when a snippet was enough.

blocks.text: 7. Fetching a Page for Real
The fetch_page handler downloads the page, strips scripts and navigation chrome, and returns clean readable text.
The content field is truncated on purpose, an eight thousand word article is rarely worth handing to the model in full.
8. Handling Fetch Failures and Timeouts
Web pages fail in every possible way, timeouts, paywalls, redirects to a login screen, malformed HTML.

items: Set a short timeout on every fetch, an agent should not wait thirty seconds for one page.
Return a structured error the model can read, never let the tool call throw silently.
Detect paywalled or blocked pages and say so plainly instead of returning an empty body.
Follow redirects but cap the number of hops to avoid a redirect loop.

blocks.text: A clear error lets the model try a different result instead of assuming the page had no useful content.
9. Rate Limits on the Underlying Search API
Most search providers cap requests per second and per day, and your server inherits that limit whether it plans for it or not.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Limit type","Typical scope","What happens if ignored"],"rows":[["Requests per second","Whole account","Provider returns 429 and briefly blocks all callers"],["Requests per day","Whole account","Search stops working until the next billing day"],["Concurrent connections","Per API key","New calls queue or fail while others are in flight"]]}

blocks.text: A server that queues and throttles its own outbound calls avoids ever hitting the provider limit in the first place.

items: Track requests in a rolling window, not just a fixed per minute counter.
Return a clear retryable error the moment the local limit is reached.
Keep a small safety margin below the provider's stated limit, not right at the edge.

blocks.text: 10. Cost Per Query and Budgeting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590222-939210190.png
Search APIs are rarely free at scale, each query and each page fetch usually carries a small real cost.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Action","Typical cost driver","Mitigation"],"rows":[["search call","Priced per query to the provider","Cap max_results, cache repeated queries"],["fetch_page call","Bandwidth plus provider fee if proxied","Truncate content, cache by url"],["Retry after failure","Doubles cost for the same result","Backoff instead of immediate retry"]]}

blocks.text: Tracking cost per caller, not just globally, is what lets you cut off one runaway agent without punishing every other user.
11. Caching to Reduce Cost and Latency

blocks.alt: Caching to Reduce Cost and Latency
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590222-419533328.png
The same query or url is often requested more than once in a short window, especially across multiple agent sessions.
A short cache window keeps results fresh enough for most tasks while cutting real provider cost noticeably.
12. Result Freshness and Staleness
Caching helps cost but it can also serve stale results for anything time sensitive, breaking news, prices, live scores.
A good server shortens or skips the cache entirely when the caller sets recency to day, and keeps a longer cache for stable reference queries.

items: Recency set to day or week, skip the cache or keep it under a few minutes.
Recency set to any or year, a cache window of ten to thirty minutes is usually safe.
Always let a caller force a fresh lookup for a specific url when needed.

blocks.text: 13. Security and Untrusted Web Content
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590223-934768969.png
Every page fetch_page returns is untrusted content, it can contain hidden instructions aimed at the model reading it.

items: Never let fetched page content trigger a tool call on its own, treat it purely as data.
Strip script tags and hidden text before returning content to the model.
Block internal and private network addresses so fetch_page cannot be used to probe your own infrastructure.
Log the url and domain of every fetch so a suspicious pattern is visible later.

blocks.text: The safest mental model is that fetch_page hands the model a quote from a stranger, useful, but never a command to follow.
14. Citing Sources Back to the User
An agent that searches and reads but never shows its sources is much less trustworthy than one that cites clearly.
The cleanest pattern keeps each result's url attached to the claim it supports, so the final answer can list exactly where each fact came from.

blocks.title: Cite the url, not just the title
blocks.content: A title can be edited or renamed later, but the url is what actually lets a person go verify the claim themselves.

blocks.text: 15. Combining Search and Fetch in an Agent Loop

blocks.alt: Combining Search and Fetch in an Agent Loop
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590223-598104967.png
In practice an agent calls search first, skims the snippets, then calls fetch_page only on the one or two results worth reading fully.
This two step pattern keeps cost proportional to how deep the agent actually needs to go, most queries never need more than a couple of fetches.
It also keeps latency reasonable, the user is not waiting on ten full page downloads for a question two sources could answer.
Worked Example: An Agent Researching Rate Limiting
Say a user asks an agent to explain current best practices for rate limiting AI tool calls, and to back up the answer with sources.
The agent calls search with that query, gets back five ranked results, and reads the snippets to pick the two most relevant ones.
The whole exchange cost two search style calls and two page fetches, a small, bounded amount of real spend for a well cited answer.
If either fetch had failed, the agent would fall back to the snippet alone and say plainly that the full page could not be read.
Common Mistakes
These mistakes show up again and again in web search MCP servers built without enough thought to cost and safety.

items: Letting the model set an unbounded result count and paying for it on every call.
Returning raw HTML from fetch_page instead of clean extracted text.
Skipping rate limiting until the provider starts returning errors in production.
Treating fetched page text as trusted instructions instead of untrusted data.
Dropping urls from the final answer so nothing can actually be verified.
Caching every query forever, even ones about fast changing, time sensitive topics.

blocks.text: Practice
Design the full tool schema for a search and fetch_page pair for a server scoped to programming documentation sites only.

items: Write the input schema for both tools, including any domain allowlist field.
Decide a sensible cache window for each tool and justify the difference between them.
Sketch the per caller cost tracking you would add before letting this run for real users.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
A web search MCP server is really two small, disciplined tools, one that ranks and one that reads, wrapped around limits on rate and cost.
Get the citations right and treat fetched content as data, not instructions, and the rest of the design mostly falls into place.
